name: Beresheet
short_status: Crashed on Mare Serenitatis during landing on 11 Apr 2019; reached lunar orbit but a reset command to a failed IMU cut the main engine. First privately funded lunar landing attempt.
tagline: SpaceIL and Israel Aerospace Industries · Lander · 2019 · Commercial and multipolar Failure
stats: Total project cost, almost entirely private
Distance flown to the Moon over ~49 days

facts.label: Launch
facts.value: 22 February 2019, 01:45 UTC, on a SpaceX Falcon 9 Block 5 from SLC-40, Cape Canaveral, as a rideshare secondary payload with the Nusantara Satu (PSN-6) telecom satellite

facts.label: Builders / operator
facts.value: SpaceIL (Israeli nonprofit, a former Google Lunar XPRIZE team) with Israel Aerospace Industries (IAI); major private financier Morris Kahn

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: 585 kg wet / 150 kg dry; roughly 1.5 m tall and 2 m across with legs deployed

facts.label: Cost
facts.value: About $100 million, overwhelmingly privately funded (Israeli government share only ~$2 million)

facts.label: Route to the Moon
facts.value: Roughly 6.5 million km over about 49 days via phasing loops around Earth, which SpaceIL/IAI describe as the longest path ever flown to the Moon (dictated by the tiny propellant load)

facts.label: Lunar orbit insertion
facts.value: 4 April 2019 (7th nation or entity, and first private venture, to orbit the Moon)

facts.label: Crash
facts.value: 11 April 2019, on Mare Serenitatis; low-angle impact (<10 degrees) at about 1,000 m/s. NASA LRO imaged the site on 22 April 2019 from 90 km altitude

facts.label: Failure cause
facts.value: During braking, one inertial measurement unit (IMU) failed; a command sent to reset it triggered a cascade that reset the main computer and shut off the main engine, which restart attempts could not recover in time

facts.label: Payloads
facts.value: NASA-provided laser retroreflector array; a magnetometer (Weizmann Institute/UCLA); a time capsule; and the Arch Mission Foundation 'Lunar Library' nanofiche archive that also carried dehydrated tardigrades

facts.label: Impact site coordinates
facts.value: 32.5956 N, 19.3496 E (LROC team solution, 95% confidence ~20 m x 8 m)

facts.label: Recognition
facts.value: Awarded the $1 million XPRIZE 'Moonshot Award' (announced 11 April 2019, presented October 2019) for reaching lunar orbit and attempting the first private landing

facts.label: Beresheet 2
facts.value: Announced 9 December 2020, the redesigned three-craft architecture (an initial Beresheet 2 concept had been floated in mid-2019); lead donors withdrew in mid-2023 and, after the funding deadline lapsed in March 2025, SpaceIL suspended engineering work in April 2025 (about 25 staff/consultants laid off), calling it a freeze rather than cancellation

timeline: Lunar orbit insertion (first private craft to orbit the Moon)
IMU failure and reset command during descent; main engine cut off; crash on Mare Serenitatis
Preliminary crash findings released (manual reset command chain)
NASA LRO images the impact site from 90 km up
LROC publishes 'Beresheet Crash Site Spotted!' with the impact coordinates
Impact study finds tardigrades unlikely to have survived ~1 km/s crash
Lead donors (Drahi, Kahn) withdraw from Beresheet 2
SpaceIL suspends Beresheet 2 development for lack of funding, calling it a freeze rather than a cancellation
